text: Customers experiencing a problem during an outage want two things fast: confirmation that the company knows, and a sense of when it'll be over. Delivering that well, on a public status page, is genuinely its own discipline — separate from the internal incident chat where the technical response is actually happening.

The habit that matters most is cadence: committing to an update on a fixed schedule, commonly every thirty minutes, whether or not there's technical progress to report. Silence between updates damages trust far more than slow progress does. And there are two opposite mistakes that both erode trust the other way — minimizing impact, calling something intermittent when it's actually widespread, which affected customers see through immediately; and over-promising a fix time before the root cause is even confirmed, since a missed ETA reads worse than no ETA at all.

Most status page tooling, from Atlassian Statuspage to incident.io, builds around the same four stages. Investigating says we know and we're on it. Identified says we found the cause. Monitoring says the fix is in and we're confirming it holds. Resolved closes the loop and sets the expectation that a fuller explanation is coming.

Internal stakeholders need a genuinely different document, not the same text trimmed down. The public page stays deliberately light on technical detail — customers don't need to know it was a bad database migration. The internal update carries the real root cause as currently understood, the actual business impact, and enough specificity for support to answer questions accurately and leadership to decide whether this needs executive attention.

Both documents are maintained by the Communications Lead, on their own cadence, because they serve different audiences and different purposes — and because someone actively debugging the problem genuinely can't also hold that discipline reliably. Next lesson turns to what happens after the incident closes: the postmortem, and how it scales across many teams instead of staying a single team's private retro.
